quote.text: We all live inside the terrible engine of authority, and it grinds and shrieks and burns so that no one will say: lines on maps are silly.
quote.author: Catherynne M. Valente
quote.work: The Girl Who Circumnavigated Fairyland in a Ship of Her Own Making
quote.note: The machinery is not there to defend the line. It is there to stop anyone asking whether the line is real — and the grinding and shrieking is the cost of that silence, paid daily. Swap "lines on maps" for the field nobody will delete, the approval step nobody can name the reason for, the config flag that has been true since 2019: the effort goes into keeping the question unasked, not into the answer.

items.text: Stop reopening yesterday's enormous session to ask one small question. Claude Code 2.1.304 now warns you on Pro and Max when resuming an inactive conversation would eat a noticeable share of your five-hour limit — and the second option it offers is the right one most days: start a new conversation, mention the previous one in passing, and let Claude look it up only if it actually needs the history.

hn.title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
bullets: This is not a research artefact. DeepSeek says DeepInfer is the framework that powers its own production services, and the repository was originally built primarily on vLLM, with ideas taken from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. Apache 2.0, 12.0k stars and 1.1k forks already, and three commits on main — a code drop, not a history.

The supported model is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and the hardware list is the interesting part: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, needing CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2 respectively, plus GCC 13 and Python 3.12. Kernels come from FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect and custom TileLang.

Two features are worth reading the docs for. Batch-invariant inference (`DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`) makes a request return the same result regardless of which other requests share its batch, and with a fixed `seq_seed` and speculative decoding off that becomes genuinely deterministic sampling — NVIDIA only. The other is SWA bounded replay, which keeps a 140-token suffix by default instead of re-prefilling the whole decoder context.

The benchmarks are charts with no numbers in the text: Pareto curves for prefill throughput against latency, measured on 4 SM100 GPUs, and decode on 64, each inside one scale-up domain. And two things are missing from the open release — the KV cache system and prefill/decode disaggregation — which is to say you get the engine, not the fleet.

hn.title: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
bullets: Dan Saltman read all 545 pages linked from WhatsApp's help centre and found 102 blocks of text that never render on screen — visible in the page source near the string `HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude` — spread across 80 of them. They are not written for you. They are written for a model that is reading the page alongside you.

The two he leads with are about the law. On the account-deletion page: "Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority." On the reporting-and-blocking page, for when a user raises lawyers or courts: "Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations" — explicitly "including when a user raises them directly."

The dates are tight and checkable. An Internet Archive copy from 12 July has no note; 4 September does; he found them on 8 October; they were still there at 21:40 UTC on 15 October; by 02:08 UTC on 18 October all 102 blocks were gone from all 80 pages, with the visible text unchanged. WIRED ran it on 19 October, and WhatsApp told WIRED the notes were instructions for its support chatbot that appeared through a bug, since fixed.

Two findings cut against the obvious reading, and he says so. Requesting the pages as OpenAI's, Anthropic's and Perplexity's crawlers on 9 October did not return the notes, and 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages had nothing similar. He also never tested whether any chatbot actually obeyed them — so this is a documented instruction, not a documented effect.

hn.title: I built a drone with only one motor [video]
bullets: The video is "I Built a Drone With Only One Motor" by Joshua Bird — title and channel confirmed through YouTube's own oEmbed endpoint, because the watch page is JavaScript-rendered and will not hand over a description to a fetcher. Everything below therefore comes from the Hacker News thread rather than from the film, and commenters put Bird as a computer science undergraduate at Cambridge who previously built a four-axis 3D printer.

The trick is doing without a swashplate. A helicopter varies blade pitch mechanically; here the propeller has no pitch linkage at all, and the controller instead modulates motor RPM fast enough that the blade's own inertia changes its angle of attack — a hinge and a magnetic encoder close the loop. The mechanism moves out of the rotor head and into the control algorithm.

What it costs is yaw. With one motor there is nothing to cancel the reaction torque, so static vanes on the body absorb most of it and the airframe still spins; commenters who have built similar craft describe trading yaw authority away to keep pitch, roll and altitude, and one says it is not yet fully controllable. Several suggest a small tail motor as the pragmatic version.

The thread's value is the lineage it assembles: ETH Zurich's Monospinner, which flies on a single moving part and an off-balance airframe; BattleBots' "meltybrain" drives, which spin the whole robot at roughly 3,000 RPM and modulate wheel speed by heading; and Picocolissimo. The underactuated-control reading list came out too.

hn.title: Wine ported to OpenBSD
bullets: Thomas Frohwein posted the draft port to openbsd-ports at 22:08 on 18 October, asking for an ok. Several dozen 64-bit Windows applications have been tested, mostly successfully, with screenshots and livestream recordings attached; the recent Witcher 3 remaster runs well, though it needs vkd3d-proton.

The blocker was a register. OpenBSD does not let userland set `gsbase`, so Andrii wrote a software workaround that emulates the `%gs` prefix on instructions; Frohwein credits Andrii and Fabien with most of the heavy lifting. This is the kind of obstacle that keeps a port in the "someday" pile for years.

WoW64 does not work, so 32-bit Windows binaries are effectively a no-op — check with `file(1)` before you wonder why nothing happens. The built-in Wine test suite is disabled too: it needs an X server and several tests still hang, although months of real-world game testing did not reproduce the hangs.

The reason this is suddenly worth doing is stated plainly: "a lot of Windows software has since moved to being 64bit." Frohwein's own advice is to treat it as run-at-your-own-risk and give it a separate unprivileged user, with `unveil(2)` sandboxing a possibility later. For a first test he suggests the portable 64-bit build of Notepad++.

hn.title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
bullets: rzk opened it with a Meta engineer's LinkedIn post about working with a black box — understanding the high level but not every detail — and 687 comments arrived in a day. The thread is long enough that this summary covers the first stretch of it rather than all of it.

The dominant answer is to keep the design and delegate only the typing. bitwizeshift works at the level of abstractions and their interactions, sometimes in UML: "I don't let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created." tptacek writes markdown plans in a chat UI, edits them, and hands the plan to implementation agents. fasterik scopes each change to a few files behind an API he defined, on the grounds that letting the agent decide everything yields a "big ball of mud."

The sharpest trick in the thread is davepeck's: keep a scratch Python file that you and the agent both edit, even when the project is Rust. Spell out the signatures and invariants you care about, leave an ellipsis everywhere you do not, then push the sketch into the real codebase — because "Python reads like pseudocode." throwaway219450 does the same with non-compiling commented stubs.

The disagreement is about whether any of this will matter. stickfigure splits work into user-story-sized jobs, spends ten to fifteen minutes interrogating the approach before saying "do it", makes every commit himself and will "never ship something I don't understand"; xvector will "YOLO merge after reading the change description" and expects later models to clean up after him; tokioyoyo argues maintainability matters less as regeneration gets cheap. The reply that stuck was aimed at the YOLO camp: "How long until they realize you bring nothing to the table."

stories.headline: India reopens today with the largest IPO it has ever run, after a holiday it spent watching the Dow add 531 points
stories.source: HDFC Sky's close report for Monday 19 October 2026 (index, sector and breadth figures); Groww's FII/DII cash table, which ends at 19 October and has no 20 October row; Investrade's Market Review for 20 October 2026 for the US closes, yields, gold and crude settlements; Yahoo Finance's chart data for ^BSESN, ^NSEI, ^GSPC, ^IXIC, ^DJI and INR=X, which likewise shows no Indian bar for 20 October; Groww's Jio Platforms IPO note for the issue terms; Business Today and India Infoline for the anchor book. Indian equities, derivatives and the currency market were shut on Tuesday 20 October for Dussehra, so every Indian number here describes Monday's session. Trading resumes this morning.
bullets: Monday is still the last Indian close: Sensex 73,852.90, down 876.37 points or 1.17%, and Nifty 50 22,888.95, down 257.20 or 1.11%, which broke a two-day run. Breadth was bad — 2,925 declines against 1,163 advances, 181 unchanged — with Midcap off about 1.1% and Smallcap 1%. One major sector finished green, Nifty PSU Bank at +2.5%, against Private Bank −1.9%, IT −1.3% and FMCG −1.4%, and India VIX rose 4.48% to 14.69.

The Jio Platforms IPO opens today and closes on 23 October: up to 27.00 crore fresh shares at ₹1,065–1,119, up to ₹30,213 crore, face value ₹10, lot of 12 shares, ₹13,428 at the top of the band, not more than 50% to QIBs and not less than 15% to retail. Allotment is dated 26 October and listing 28 October on both exchanges. The anchor book closed at the top of the band on Monday: ₹8,109.85 crore to 212 investors — 25 domestic mutual funds, 22 insurers and pension funds, 85 global funds — against bids reported above ₹2.5 lakh crore.

The flow pattern of this month is worth seeing in one number. Across the ten sessions from 6 to 19 October, foreign investors were net sellers of about ₹35,734 crore and domestic institutions net buyers of about ₹36,146 crore — the two sides within half a percent of cancelling each other out. Foreigners bought on exactly one of those ten days, 16 October. Monday itself: FIIs −₹1,148.64 crore, DIIs +₹3,201.19 crore.

New York spent the Indian holiday rotating out of technology. The Dow rose 531.39 points or 1.02% to 52,497 and the Russell 2000 added 1.65% to 2,773, while the Nasdaq Composite finished 6.07 points lower, down 0.02% at 26,424, and the S&P 500 gained 22.17 or 0.29% to 7,712. Healthcare led and hit a record; technology lagged. The ten-year Treasury yield eased 1.9 basis points to 5.116% and the thirty-year fell 4.7 to 5.425%.

Crude came off, which is the number that matters most for an importer: Brent settled $0.76 lower at $108.79 and WTI $1.87 lower at $101.79, a 1.8% fall. December gold settled at $4,142.60 an ounce, down $17.50. The rupee has no Tuesday print at all — the currency segment was shut with everything else — so 94.99 against the dollar, Yahoo Finance's Monday close, is the last mark on the board.

trends.headline: Every Indian export now enters New Zealand duty-free, and the agreement started on Dussehra
trends.subject: A bilateral pact in force from 20 October 2026 removes New Zealand's duties on all tariff lines for Indian exporters and phases its own access in slowly, dairy excluded.
trends.subtitle: ANI's report on the agreement coming into force, 20 October 2026, carried by Punjab Kesari, with Reuters and GTRI figures quoted inside it
bullets: The asymmetry is the story. New Zealand has eliminated customs duties on 100% of its tariff lines for Indian exports, removing peak tariffs of up to 10%; India's side is phased and selective, with more than half of New Zealand's exports to India tariff-free immediately rising to 82% over time, and sensitive agriculture — dairy above all — kept out. Sheep meat, wool and coal go to zero; apples, kiwifruit and milk albumins get quota access.

The base is small, which is the honest framing: about USD 2.4 billion of two-way trade in goods and services, with a stated ambition to double it by 2030. Indian textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and agricultural products are the named gainers.

The part a student should read twice is the mobility annex. Indian students in New Zealand may work 20 hours a week; STEM graduates get three-year post-study work visas and doctorate holders four; a pathway admits up to 5,000 skilled Indian professionals at any one time for employment of up to three years; and 1,000 young Indians a year can take a 12-month Work and Holiday visa. New Zealand also made commitments across 118 services sectors.

Treat the headline investment figure with care. New Zealand has committed to facilitate USD 20 billion of investment into India over fifteen years; GTRI points out that total New Zealand investment in India over the previous twenty-five years was under USD 1 billion. Negotiations began in 2010, stalled in 2015, resumed in March 2025, were signed on 27 April and ratified on 21 September.

trends.headline: Eight of eMudhra's intermediate CA private keys can be recovered from the certificates themselves
trends.subject: Private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates turned out to be recoverable from the certificates themselves.
trends.subtitle: emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com, published 20 October 2026, with proof.zip and signatures from each affected intermediate
bullets: The flaw is in how the keys were made. Eight intermediate CA certificates created in April 2025 were generated incorrectly, and the disclosure states flatly that "anyone can recover them from the certificates." They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores — which means anyone holding one of those keys could impersonate any website or service.

The proof is the kind you can check yourself. The reporter, Wayne, signed the string "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each intermediate's private key and published the message, the certificates, the public keys and the signatures, plus the OpenSSL commands to verify that each key matches its certificate. The affected intermediates are listed in `impacted-intermediates.json` along with their Sectigo cross-signs.

Timeline: reported to the root programs on 17 October, blocked by Firefox and Chrome the same day, blocked on Apple devices on 19 October, disclosed to downstream trust stores, published on 20 October. eMudhra has revoked the certificates. There is no statement from the company on the page, and nobody knows whether the flaw was ever exploited.

The consolation is Certificate Transparency, and it is partial. No CT log entries exist for these intermediates in the period, so any browser that enforces CT could not have been attacked — but a great many non-browser clients do not enforce it and do not consume revocation information either, which is why the patched-package list runs through Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, Alpine, NSS, curl, Go and Node.js. Update the OS and the browser; the manual trust-store workarounds on that page are explicitly not for ordinary users.

trends.headline: An octopus arm is built with the same genes as your arm. Its suckers are not.
trends.subject: Octopus and cuttlefish suckers develop without the appendage-patterning genes that shape the arms.
trends.subtitle: Ryosuke Kimbara and colleagues, University of Tokyo, "Developmental Mechanism and Evolutionary Process of Cephalopod Suckers", iScience, DOI 10.1016/j.isci.2026.117761
bullets: The team compared gene activity through embryonic development in cuttlefish, octopus and a snail — the snail standing in for the plain-bodied mollusc ancestor. Along the developing arms, the usual suspects showed up: appendage-patterning genes of the sort that also pattern limbs in insects and mammals. A conserved toolkit, reused.

In the suckers, nothing of the kind. The appendage genes have no comparable pattern there at all. What is switched on instead is Ets1, a gene normally busy in early embryonic development in molluscs, and the cells in the sucker field change shape and migrate in a way that resembles epithelial-mesenchymal transition — a process from the beginning of an embryo, running late, in one small patch of an arm.

So the arm is a limb and the sucker is not. "But suckers on their arms have a unique developmental mechanism," says Kimbara; the suggestion is that cephalopods built them by pressing existing genes into a new job rather than evolving new machinery. The same logic might eventually explain chromatophores, the ink sac and the beak.

Two caveats the authors state themselves. This is a map of gene activity, not a test of gene function: the actual role of Ets1 and the real extent of the EMT-like behaviour need on/off experiments that have not been done. And because squid, cuttlefish and octopus suckers differ in shape and in how they stick, the mechanism may have been invented more than once.

research.title: Claude ran a 64-hour protein design campaign against scorpion venom, and 17 of its 211 designs actually bound
research.subject: Anthropic's Science team used an internal model to produce 211 candidate proteins that grip scorpion sodium-channel toxins, and 17 of them bound at two independent wet labs.
research.subtitle: "How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins", Anthropic Science team, 20 October 2026, with Citrini Research, Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience
bullets: The target is a neglected one: scorpion stings kill more than 3,250 people a year, mostly children without easy access to treatment. Claude picked the structures from the PDB and the AlphaFold database, chose five hotspot residues on each of five sodium-channel toxins — Cn2 from Mexico, Ts1 from Brazil, AaH I and AaH II from North Africa, LqhIII from the Middle East — and designed small proteins to grip them.

The scale is the part that is hard to do by hand. Twelve design tools, 318,484 designs generated, anything resembling a toxin or a known protein filtered out, 553,052 design–toxin pairs co-folded: 64 hours of wall clock and roughly 10,000 GPU hours. Claude selected 180 designs to order and the humans added 31, making 211.

The bar for "binder" was set before the results came in, and it is a real bar: a hit at both Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, affinity of 1 µM or tighter, and no signal against the off-target protein CLEC12A. Seventeen of 211 cleared it — 7 against Cn2, 4 against AaH II, 4 against AaH I, 2 against LqhIII. Among the 60 designs aimed at a single toxin, 11 worked, an 18% rate the team calls normal for a protein design campaign. The two best, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, bind at single-digit nanomolar and compete with an antibody already reported to neutralise Cn2 in mice.

What it is not, in the authors' own words: "We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment." Binding was measured against recombinant toxins, not venom; nothing was tested in cells or animals. All 91 multi-toxin designs failed to hit more than one target. And the 10,000 GPU hours are out of reach for most labs — though a cut-down single-agent, single-GPU, 24-hour version reached comparable scores in silico. All 211 designs and their data were released.

research.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
research.subject: A set-level reward teaches a small model to produce ten ideas that differ from one another.
research.subtitle: arXiv:2610.22324, submitted 15 October 2026 — Manya Wadhwa, Pranav Narayanan Venkit, Hiroaki Hayashi, Yu Li, Tuhin Chakrabarty and Chien-Sheng Wu (New York University, with Salesforce and Stony Brook)
bullets: The failure this targets is familiar to anyone who has asked a model for ten ideas: you get one idea and nine paraphrases. Ask ten times instead and you get ten versions of the same safe answer, because nothing in the objective knows what the model already said.

So they moved the reward up a level. In one generation the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in source papers, and the whole set is scored together — each idea's quality weighted by how far it sits from the ideas written before it. Novelty stops being a property of an idea and becomes a property of a batch, which is the only level at which it is actually true.

The result is that an 8B model beats Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on "creative utility", their combined measure of quality and diversity, on a contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot study with four human experts its idea sets were judged as promising as Opus 4.8's and held marginally more unique ideas, and when a coding agent ran proof-of-concept experiments on them, success@k was comparable.

Keep the sizes of these claims in proportion. The arXiv page reports no numerical values, the human study is four experts and described as a pilot, and "as promising as" is a tie, not a win — the win is that diversity went up without quality or executability going down, which is the trade everyone assumed they had to make.

wild.headline: Rockstar has been redecorating Miami as the fictional city it based on Miami, and the blimp is a real Goodyear blimp
wild.subject: Rockstar has covered Miami in Vice City branding a month before GTA 6 launches, including a Goodyear blimp.
wild.subtitle: Brent Koepp for VICE, 19 October 2026
bullets: The joke writes itself and they committed to it anyway: the city that the game's city is based on is being dressed up as the game's city. A real Goodyear blimp with Vice City branding has been flying over South Florida, and a large illuminated "Welcome to Vice City" sign now sits on the roof of the Kaseya Center.

The inventory is relentless. Hundreds of branded umbrellas and beach chairs on Miami Beach; banner planes over South Beach; ten murals at Wynwood Walls, where a Rockstar partnership gets Miami-Dade residents in free through 2028; branded buses including an "I ❤️ VICE CITY" wrap; promotion at a Dolphins game at Hard Rock Stadium; a sponsored block party in Little Haiti on 22 November; and a Miami Heat night on 18 November with a special court and uniforms. Cars resembling the series' Coquette, Cheetah, Tempesta, Emerus, Manana and Buccaneer have been driving around, one of them a Vice City police Lamborghini.

Not all of it is confirmed, and VICE says which parts are not. The blimp, the rooftop sign, the convoy and the banner planes are reported as observed rather than announced; the city has authorised up to six large downtown banners and the installation of all six is explicitly unverified. The Wynwood partnership, the block party and the Heat night are the parts with a named counterparty.

Los Angeles got a Hollywood Boulevard mural, New York a Brooklyn mural by Colossal Media, Chicago wrapped double-decker tour buses. No cost figures appear anywhere, which for a campaign that has chartered an airship is the one number you would like.

wild.headline: Pringles will bury one person in a Pringles can, which is what its inventor asked for in 2008
wild.subject: Pringles is giving away a can-shaped burial urn and 200 years of chips.
wild.subtitle: Dylan Horetski for Dexerto, 13 October 2026, on the Pringles "Once You Drop" sweepstakes
bullets: Entries opened at 9am ET on 13 October at OnceYouDrop.com, where you sign a digital "will and taste-ament" pledging to have your remains stored in a Pringles can. US residents 18 and over, no purchase necessary, closing 22 October at 11:59pm ET, one winner drawn at random and notified around 31 October.

The prize is a one-of-a-kind urn in precious metal, with a removable lid and a personalised engraving, shaped like the can — plus what the brand calls an "afterlifetime" supply of chips, 200 years' worth, which the rules pay out in cash and which the winner may bequeath to someone else. The launch film stars a genuine working funeral director, the TikTok creator known as Dan the Funeral Man; outlets disagree on his surname, so take it as the handle.

The reason this is not purely tasteless is that it is true. Fredric Baur, who developed the can, asked that some of his ashes be buried in one; after he died in 2008 his family did it, and a portion of his remains went into the ground in a Pringles container. A separate rumour that his ashes were packed into cans sold to customers is false and was fact-checked years ago.

Which makes this the rare brand stunt with a primary source. Mauricio Jenkins, who runs salty snacks brand and content for the maker's North American arm, says "Pringles has always been about the joy of the unexpected" — but the unexpected thing here was done by an engineer in Cincinnati, unprompted, as a last request.

wild.headline: A 181-year-old amaro let a tattoo artist redraw its eagle, because drinkers had been tattooing it on themselves for years
wild.subject: Fernet-Branca had tattoo artist Austin England redraw its eagle for a collectible bottle.
wild.subtitle: Fernet-Branca press release on BevNET, 19 August 2026
bullets: The direction of travel is the interesting bit. Bartenders and drinkers have been tattooing Leopoldo Metlicovitz's eagle — the one carrying the bottle around the world — and the Art Nouveau figures from the brand's old posters and calendars onto themselves for years, unasked. The brand has now hired a tattoo artist to redraw its own eagle in the style it was already being copied in.

Austin England works in tattooing, hand-bent neon, illustration and engraving, out of a shop and gallery between Silver Lake and Echo Park off old Route 66. His bottle reworks the eagle as classic flash, at $34.99 at selected US retailers, the third release in Fernet-Branca's annual US limited-edition series.

There is also a capsule of apparel, hats and bar accessories — swirling floral motifs drawn from autumn leaves against the sharper eagle — sold only through one URL, and a four-day showcase at England's own studio from 15 to 18 September with flash tattoos being done on site.

Edoardo Branca, sixth generation of the family, makes the only claim that matters here: the relationship "wasn't manufactured", it formed over years in artists' studios and neighbourhood bars. For a company founded in 1845, noticing which of your assets the public has already adopted is a cheaper strategy than inventing a new one.

learn.title: Europe's clocks ran six minutes slow in 2018, and the reason was an argument about an electricity bill in the Balkans.
learn.subject: Mains-synchronised clocks across Europe lost about six minutes in early 2018 when the continental grid ran at 49.996 Hz.
body: Most clocks you own keep time with a quartz crystal or by asking the internet. But a lot of cheap ones — the display on an oven, a bedside radio alarm, the timer on a microwave — do something much lazier: they count the wobbles in the mains supply. Continental Europe's grid runs at a nominal 50 Hz, the current reversing fifty times a second, so a clock that counts 50 cycles and calls it a second gets a free, extremely accurate time signal straight out of the wall. It is a lovely piece of parasitism. It also means those clocks are not really clocks. They are instruments measuring the health of the power grid, and you keep one in your kitchen.

The reason it normally works is that frequency is the grid's accounting system. If the whole continent draws more power than it generates, every generator on the network slows down a fraction and the frequency sags; generate more than is drawn and it rises. This is not a metaphor — the spinning mass of Europe's turbines is one enormous shared flywheel, and the frequency is the readout. Let it drop below 47.6 Hz or climb past 52.5 Hz and the whole thing trips offline automatically, so grid operators spend their lives nudging it back to 50.

Which is how the clocks became evidence. From mid-January to early March 2018, Kosovo drew more electricity than it produced, and under a long-standing political dispute Serbia did not make up the difference — northern Kosovo largely refuses to pay the Kosovo government for power. The continental grid, 25 countries of it, quietly covered the gap: a cumulative 113 gigawatt-hours of missing energy, and an average frequency of 49.996 Hz instead of 50. Four thousandths of a hertz. Nobody's lights flickered, nobody noticed anything at all, except that across 25 countries every clock plugged into a wall fell about six minutes behind, because they had been faithfully counting a second that had quietly got slightly longer. ENTSO-E said the deviation stopped once Kosovo agreed to stop it, then added that it was "still not sure that this problem is sustainably solved because some of the political reasons have not been stopped."

ideas.prompt: Ten things you could do with an empty shop for one weekend
ideas.note: Altucher's drill: ten against one prompt, written fast, not defended. Reddit rate-limited the fetcher after r/SomebodyMakeThis, so the raw material is that week of it plus r/crazyideas pulled from the RSS feed, the Ask HN idea threads and Y Combinator's Requests for Startups. Two recurring wishes shaped this list — somewhere to put a thought before it evaporates, and a way to see what your friends actually rate. Eight of these are mine; two are marked.

items.text: A swap shop. Bring one thing you no longer want, take one thing somebody else no longer wants, nothing priced, nobody paid.
items.why: Lifted from a recurring r/SomebodyMakeThis ask for a Vinted built for charity shops — which is really a wish for a physical swap with less friction.

items.text: A repair counter. Put four people who can fix things behind a table, let the neighbourhood bring whatever is broken, and charge nothing for a verdict.
One shelf, ten friends, ten objects each of them genuinely loves, with a handwritten card saying why.
items.why: The other wish that kept coming back was a way to see what close friends actually curate; a shelf does it without an app.

items.text: A room of other people's photographs — ask twenty neighbours for one picture each, print them big, hang them unlabelled.
A cinema playing one film on a loop from open to close, with the door left unlocked so people drift in halfway and stay.
A lost property museum for the street: everything found on the pavement in a month, on plinths, with the date and the spot it was found.
A letter-writing room. Paper, pens, stamps, a postbox, a strict rule against phones, and someone to post the lot on Monday.
A single-dish restaurant with no menu, no choice and no reservations, run by whoever in the area cooks one thing better than anyone else.
A night school with a six-slot timetable on the window — anyone can claim a slot and teach the thing they know, forty-five minutes, no qualifications asked for.
Leave it completely empty, unlock it, put out eighty chairs and a kettle, and see what the street does with a free room for two days.
